articles.author: Stuart Heritage
articles.title: ‘The brains of a pea and the mouth of diarrhoea!’ It’s the wildest I’m a Celebrity spats
articles.description: Mariella Frostrup is facing a backlash after blowing up in the camp. It’s not the first time a stranded star’s tongue has caused a row – and some of them have been truly pathetic The unique selling point of I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! is that it is currently the only show on television where you get to watch animal abuse and reputation-destroying arguments at the same time. The former is an ongoing affair, with petitions and boycotts rumbling on as always. But the latter has just exploded, thanks to Mariella Frostrup and all her microaggressions. If you haven’t been watching, and in this day and age why would you, here’s a brief precis. Last Thursday, latecomer AJ Odudu offered to help Frostrup cook a meal, which Frostrup took as unwelcome criticism of her skills. But when they cooked together the following night, things went badly, Frostrup snapped and Odudu cried. But last night, during an attempt to clear the air, Frostrup said she had actually been glad to have had help. Odudu’s’s reply was essentially that she had a funny way of showing it, to which Frostrup replied: “You see, that’s just aggressive and that’s what keeps happening.” Odudu’s response was to sigh: “Please don’t use those words towards me.” Nevertheless, the altercation was enough for Frostrup to be called to the Bush Telegraph so producers could “discuss why what was said might make someone uncomfortable, how to address it, and how to move forward.” Continue reading...

Full year completions were 1,353, at the bottom end of the Group’s previous guidance range of 1,350 to 1,400 completions. The warning has hammered Crest Nicholson shares, which have lost more than a quarter of their value this morning, currently trading down over 30%. The brutal sell-off is also weighing on the wider sector, dragging peers like Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Vistry and Bellway into the red. Today’s update suggests that weakness in the housing market is no longer confined to first-time buyers. Crest Nicholson is predominantly exposed to the mid-premium family housing market, and the sharp deterioration in sales rates indicates that more affluent upsizers are also becoming increasingly cautious amid macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jonathan Wilson
articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino can now see just how desperate Manchester United are | Jonathan Wilson
articles.description: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...

articles.author: Brian Logan
articles.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
articles.description: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. Continue reading...

articles.author: Kate Lloyd
articles.title: Is it true that … we only use 10% of our brains?
articles.description: The idea that we access a fraction of our cognitive potential goes back decades, but does medical science agree? This idea really bugs Dr Mary Spiller , senior lecturer in the University of East London’s Department of Psychology and Human Development, who’s shocked by how prevalent it remains, despite being untrue. Spiller says the myth’s origins can partly be traced to the work of William James, one of the founders of modern psychology, working in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He wrote: “We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Helen Pilcher
articles.title: Nasa is looking for new astronauts to send to the moon, and I know who’d be perfect for the job: middle-aged women like me | Helen Pilcher
articles.description: We’ve been training for this mission for years – solving problems, defusing tensions, keeping everyone fed – and we’d absolutely smash it Nasa is hiring and I’m over the moon. The US space agency is recruiting its next cohort of astronauts to work on the lunar surface and “help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure”. Applications close on 3 December. This isn’t the only job I’ve been swooning over lately. I can’t tell you how many hours I’ve lost to posts about deliciously distant jobs: running the world’s southernmost post office in Antarctica, where staff double as penguin counters, or minding the Great Blasket island off the coast of County Kerry, where the northern lights sometimes shimmer over the North Atlantic. All of it bathed in a warm, rosy glow. In our always-on world, swapping the inbox for an island – or, for the truly frazzled, the moon – seems less like a job and more like a wellness retreat. Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side Effects Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.author: Stuart Clark
articles.title: Starwatch: a rare chance to observe elusive Mercury
articles.description: Being so close to the sun, the smallest planet in the solar system is also one of the most difficult to spot This week offers a good opportunity to spot Mercury, the smallest planet in the solar system and one of the most difficult to observe. On 20 November, it reached “greatest western elongation”, the point at which it appears farthest from the sun in the morning sky. The planet remains well placed for observation over the next few mornings. The chart shows the view looking east-south-east from London at 0630 GMT on 24 November. Mercury appears low above the horizon, while the much brighter planet Venus shines higher in the sky, close to Spica, the brightest star in the constellation of Virgo, the virgin. Continue reading...
